_readme: THE COMPONENT CATALOGUE. Parts, with dimensions, each tracing to a source.
JSON and not JavaScript on purpose: LoopBench is Python and must read these
same rows. A JS table would force a second copy, which is the disease the
netlist exists to cure. See 00 - Project/Process Core — Component Catalogue.md.
EVERY dimension carries BOTH the value as printed in its standard AND the
canonical conversion. test/catalogue.test.js re-derives one from the other and
fails on a slip, so an arithmetic error cannot enter silently.
Canonical unit is INCHES. No part holds a pixel, a colour or a behaviour.
SEEDED FROM WHAT IS HELD, which is process-industry. It does NOT yet serve
Lunar Process Engineer level 1, which is an agricultural rig -- microirrigation,
governed by ASABE or the ISO irrigation series, neither of which is in hand.
Emerson's enterprise agreement carries no agricultural body at all (checked
2026-10-10). That errand is open and is not an ASME one.

units.note: as-printed values keep their own unit

_source.table: flow coefficient tables, ED / EZ / EW globe families
note: Fisher Catalog 12 prints, for every valve size and port, the port
diameter and the maximum rated travel in BOTH millimetres and inches,
which is exactly the pairing this catalogue requires -- so these rows
arrive already carrying their own evidence. The extraction found the
pairs by their 25.4 ratio in the first place; keeping both halves is
declining to throw away what the reader already had to use.
cv is the measured curve at every 10% of travel, and belongs here
rather than in a consumer: it is what the part IS, in the same sense
as its port diameter, and the trim layer reads it the way the
geometry layer reads a bore.
characterisedBy distinguishes the two archetypes. ED/ET/EW are
cage-characterised. EZ is not: D100401X012 names a "seat ring retainer
and bushing assembly" throughout and never a cage, and the
characteristic comes from the bottom bevel of the plug. They are
different parts to draw and the distinction is not recoverable from
the numbers alone, so it is recorded.
flow is null wherever the sheet does not state it. The ED IOM says
standard cages are "normally down" -- normally is not always, and a
guess here would silently flip which chamber is the inlet.
NOT here: rotary bodies (Vee-Ball, Control-Disk, V500), and the
Catalog 12 pages those live on. Named so nobody reads this group as
the whole catalogue.

_source.table: 5.1.1 Face-to-Face Dimensions for Flanged, Globe-Style Control Valves
note: Control Valve Handbook 6th ed., section 5.1.1, "Face-to-Face
Dimensions for Flanged, Globe-Style Control Valves". The Handbook
states these follow a part of the ISA-75.08 series, but the HANDBOOK
is what is held and read -- no part of that series has been opened,
and its register entry says so, along with which part covers which
body style.
Printed in millimetres AND inches, which is the pairing this
catalogue requires, so these rows carry their own evidence.
NOT here: the Classes 900/1500/2500 table, which prints a SHORT and
a LONG dimension per size and is a different shape of row; and
sections 5.1.2 to 5.1.6 -- butt weld, socket weld, screwed, angle,
and separable flange ends.
DROPPED, not corrected: NPS 14 Class 600 RTJ. The Handbook prints
475 mm beside 38.37 in; 38.37 in is 975 mm. The page image was
rendered to confirm it is the book and not the text extraction.
Writing 975 would replace a printed number with a guessed one, so
the row is left out and the extractor names it on every run.

_note: WHAT A FITTING COSTS. Not a number -- a correlation, evaluated at the
Reynolds number and bore in play. Two are held and they disagree, so
both are carried and the caller chooses; see src/sizing.js for which
is the outlier at which size.
THE JUDGEMENT THIS FORCES, stated here rather than buried in code:
NO PUBLISHED CORRELATION HAS A SOCKET-WELD ROW. The choice is
'threaded' or 'flanged/welded', and for ASME B16.11 fittings the
honest mapping is THREADED -- B16.11 governs socket-welding AND
threaded fittings in one document and gives them the same body
dimensions, Table 1 and Table 5 carrying the same centre-to-bottom-of-
socket A. They are the same forging with a different end preparation,
and both are compact blocks with sharp internal corners. A flanged or
butt-welded elbow has a real radius, which is exactly why its
coefficient is lower.
If anything this UNDER-states the loss: a socket-weld joint leaves a
small annular step at the socket bottom that a threaded one does not.
No source quantifies it, so it is not modelled -- recorded, not guessed.
Every basis carries its uncertainty. Published fitting-loss data runs
25-30% in general and 10% at the very best.

TEE/RUN/THREADED.appliesTo: tee-socketweld, flow straight through the run

TEE/BRANCH/THREADED.appliesTo: tee-socketweld, flow turning out of the branch

hooper-2k.source: Hooper 2-K, tee used as elbow, screwed

note: VIA the Control Valve Handbook 6th ed., chapter 14 Pipe Data, which is
what the vault actually holds. ASME B36.10M itself is registered and has
never been opened -- its register entry says so -- and recording this as
the standard would claim a document nobody here has read.
Seeded at NPS 1/8 to 10 because the department serves power, nuclear,
refining and severe service. The catalogue previously stopped at NPS 1/2,
which is a grow bay, not a refinery.
NPS 12 and larger are NOT here: the Handbook chapter continues on pages
the reader does not match. Named so nobody assumes completeness.
Every row satisfies bore = od - 2*wall to the printed precision, which is
how the reader found them at all. The nominal size column is merged across
schedules, and carrying it forward silently produced NPS 8 bores wearing
NPS 6 labels.
`nps` is NUMERIC so a fitting can be matched to its pipe; `npsLabel` keeps
the printed form, because 1.25 and 1-1/4 are the same size and only one of
them is what anybody writes on a drawing.

_source.title: Socket-Welding Elbows, Tees, and Crosses
note: A socket-welding 90 degree elbow is a COMPACT FORGED BLOCK, not a sweeping
curve. The dimension that locates it is centre-to-bottom-of-socket, A --
how far from the fitting's centre the pipe end lands. There is no long
radius at this size.
Tee and cross share the elbow's A at the same NPS and class.

_source.title: Dimensions of Long Radius Elbows
_source.printedUnit: mm (in.) -- both columns, and the INCH one is what the standard asserts
note: Centre-to-end; for a 90 degree elbow this IS the centreline radius.
The 1.5 x NPS rule holds only from NPS 1 upward -- below that the
dimension floors at a flat 1.50 in. The table STARTS at NPS 1/2, so
there is no buttweld elbow for NPS 3/8 at all.
Buttwelding is not used at small bore: see ASME B16.11 instead.

_note: A material is the axis a pressure rating hangs on, not a label.
These carry NO dimensions yet: ASME B16.34's material-group and
pressure-temperature tables have not been opened, and the ASTM product
specs themselves are not in the register at all. What is recorded is
identity and where the answer lives -- which is honest, and is what lets
a part say what it is made of before anyone has read the rating tables.
